items.title: Kenny Burrell — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I come out just to explore and all of a sudden the phone rings and it’s Jimmy Jones and a couple of other guys. They said, “Hey man, we’re coming over here to see you.”

ctx.x: So you’re here in ’71, now we’re in Los Angeles, you made it across the coast, or from coast to coast. So that was, did you have a goal coming out here, other than raising your family, as far as a career goal? Were you interested in continuing your career as a bandleader, or were you going to continuing the diversity of working…

Right, as a bandleader and as a recording artist. So I would go up to make, I say maybe two albums a year. And then I started to record with other people for Fantasy, Gene Ammons and ‘cause Sam Russell was my good friend, he was a kind of a contractor for Gene. And my good buddy Sam and he did some records with Lorez Alexandria and, you know, as a producer and I did a few dates for him. But, no, I just wanted to enjoy this area and take advantage of the opportunity and more or less do what I was doing in New York…

Okay, before we take that on, as far as your educational career because I really want to focus on that and talk about not only your career… Burrell:…trajectory but also talk about how you’ve developed your curriculum and you pedagogy. I want to talk about, the reason why I asked about your career goals coming out to L.A. because this is, forgive me, Hollyweird, Hollywood. And you’ve already done the soundtrack of Pawnbroker with Quincy, that was done in the in the mid 60’s…

items.title: 69537_Jimmy Jones oral history interview
items.q: I talked with Kenny about it... He says it's good, man... Kenny and I talked about that, too... I was telling Kenny Burrell... when we were speaking about the piano solo

ctx.x: Kenny Burrell, -- let's see, I forget who was playing bass.
I do too. I just remember you and Kenny. And Sarah.
